query: For high-entropy-alloy protective coatings in wear-resistant applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their wear performance and why? Define a controlled change that would distinguish the hypothesis from a baseline, the directional observations expected if it is correct, the range over which it should hold, the prior evidence that supports it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Below a critical nanograin size (around 30 nm), HEA coatings undergo a dynamic transition that forms an ultra-nanocrystalline or amorphous near-surface layer during sliding, resulting in lower shear strength (inverse Hall–Petch behavior) and thereby significantly reducing friction coefficients and wear rates.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy coating (e.g., CoCrFeMnNi) deposited with a coarse-grained microstructure (>30 nm grain size) that does not exhibit dynamic amorphization under wear.
generation.intervention: Systematically adjust processing parameters (e.g., cooling rate or milling time) to produce HEA coatings with controlled nanograin sizes spanning above and below the ~30 nm threshold.
generation.conditions: Perform wear tests under controlled sliding conditions (constant normal load, speed, and inert or ultra-high vacuum environment to minimize oxidative effects) to isolate the mechanical effects of grain size refinement.
generation.structural_mediator: The wear-induced formation of an ultrananocrystalline/amorphous surface layer that is triggered when the bulk nanograin size is below the critical threshold.
generation.mechanism: When the grain size falls below ~30 nm, dislocation-mediated plasticity is suppressed and grain boundary sliding becomes the dominant deformation mode. This dynamic amorphization at the surface lowers local shear strength (inverse Hall–Petch effect), yielding reduced friction and wear compared to coatings with larger grains.
generation.predicted_outcome: HEA coatings with grain sizes below ~30 nm will develop a dynamic amorphous or ultra-nanocrystalline surface layer during sliding, which will exhibit considerably lower friction coefficients and specific wear rates than those with coarser grain structures.
generation.baseline: HEA coatings with coarse grain sizes (>30 nm) that do not undergo the dynamic formation of an amorphous surface layer during wear.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is predicted to hold under dry sliding conditions in inert environments (e.g., UHV) and at moderate temperatures where oxidative effects are minimal. Variations in alloy chemistry or extreme testing temperatures may alter the critical threshold or mechanism.
generation.uncertainty: The exact critical grain size threshold may vary with the specific HEA composition and processing history, and the degree of dynamic amorphization may depend on subtle changes in testing conditions. Further, non-mechanistic factors (such as tribo-oxidation in reactive environments) are not considered.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate a series of HEA coatings where the nanograin size is systematically varied across the ~30 nm threshold by altering processing conditions. Conduct identical sliding wear tests in an inert (or ultra-high vacuum) environment while measuring friction coefficient and wear rate. Post-test, use TEM and related surface characterization techniques to verify the presence and extent of an amorphous or ultra-nanocrystalline surface layer.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If coatings with nanograin sizes below ~30 nm do not exhibit the formation of a dynamic amorphous or ultra-nanocrystalline layer, or if their friction coefficients and wear rates are not significantly lower than those of coatings with larger grains, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties

A plot of grain size-dependent shear strength for CoCrFeMnNi is shown in Fig. 2, including data from a systematic investigation of Hall-Petch behavior from Liu, et al. and an estimate in the nanocrystalline regime (grain size ca. 80 nm) from a torsional severe plastic deformation (SPD) investigation by Schuh, et al.. The Hall-Petch equation, σy=σ0+k⋅d−1/2, is fit to the Luo data only, and agrees reasonably well with the nano-grained estimate from Schuh, et al.. Recent work has shown that low friction of bare metals, in the range μ≅0.2−0.5, can be explained as the dynamic softening (i.e. inverse Hall-Petch behavior) of surfaces due to highly surface-localized, shear-induced severe plastic deformation,,. This is well described by a recently proposed predictive model that explains the low shear strength and friction coefficients of bare metals and alloys. This model of grain size-dependent shear strength requires no fitting parameters and is based exclusively on materials properties and physically meaningful input parameters like temperature and shear rate. frame.goal: Understand the underlying mechanistic behavior that governs the wear performance of these coatings in service conditions.
frame.limitation: There is a lack of a single, testable mechanistic hypothesis that clearly isolates the role of microstructural or chemical features in determining wear resistance.

decision.trend: Early work on HEA coatings established empirical correlations between bulk hardness or phase content and wear rate. In subsequent studies, researchers began to uncover mechanistic effects – for instance, PMC7311485 highlighted a dynamic amorphization process and demonstrated an inverse Hall–Petch behavior, connecting grain size refinement to low friction and wear. Most recently (as seen in PMC10241162), efforts have shifted toward engineering nanohierarchical architectures that adapt under wear, yet these experiments still largely rely on correlational evidence rather than isolating a single microstructural factor as the driver.
decision.unsolved: A clear, controlled, and quantitatively testable hypothesis that identifies a single microstructural lever – such as a critical grain-size threshold for dynamic amorphization – governing the wear performance of HEA coatings across different tribological regimes remains undefined.
decision.lever: Systematically vary the nanograin size (by adjusting processing parameters like cooling rate or milling time) to cross a hypothesized critical threshold (around 30 nm) that triggers a dynamic transition (amorphization) in the wear-induced surface layer
decision.why: Prior mechanistic studies (e.g., PMC7311485) imply that below a certain grain size the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline/amorphous layer dramatically reduces friction and wear. A controlled experiment that isolates nanograin size will test whether this transition is the key mechanistic driver, thereby directly addressing the knowledge gap and providing a falsifiable, quantitative hypothesis.
